questions.q: Define depreciation in one sentence using the terms "depreciable cost", "useful life", and "expired cost".
questions.a: Depreciation is the systematic allocation of the depreciable cost of a tangible fixed asset over its estimated useful life, representing the expired cost charged as an expense each period. A wrong answer (e.g., "depreciation is the fall in market value") reveals the student confuses accounting depreciation (cost allocation) with economic depreciation (market value change) – a critical distinction because accounting depreciation is based on historical cost, not market fluctuations.

questions.q: A student says: "Depreciation is charged so that we have cash to replace the asset when it wears out." Explain why this statement is incorrect and what the true purpose of depreciation is.
questions.a: Depreciation is a non-cash expense; it does not generate cash. Its purpose is to match the expired cost of the asset to the revenue it helps generate (matching principle), ensuring true profit measurement. A student who thinks depreciation creates a replacement fund confuses depreciation (an expense) with a sinking fund or reserve (an appropriation of profit). This misconception leads to errors in cash flow analysis and profit calculation.

questions.q: Classify each of the following as depreciation, depletion, or amortisation: (a) A coal mine purchased for ₹2 crore, (b) A patent acquired for ₹50 lakh, (c) A factory building costing ₹10 crore. Justify each classification in one line.
questions.a: (a) Depletion – exhaustion of natural resource. (b) Amortisation – expiry of intangible asset's legal life. (c) Depreciation – wear and tear/obsolescence of tangible fixed asset. A wrong classification (e.g., calling the patent "depreciation") shows the student cannot distinguish asset types: tangible vs. intangible vs. wasting assets. This matters because AS-6 treats them similarly but terminology differs.

questions.q: A company purchases a machine for ₹5,00,000 (installation ₹50,000) with a 10-year life and ₹50,000 scrap value. The accountant debits the full ₹5,50,000 to Profit & Loss in Year 1. Analyse the impact on (i) Year 1 profit, (ii) Year 2–10 profits, (iii) Balance Sheet asset value, and (iv) Tax liability in Year 1.
questions.a: (i) Year 1 profit understated by ₹4,95,000 (₹5,50,000 – ₹55,000 depreciation). (ii) Year 2–10 profits overstated by ₹55,000 each year (no depreciation charged). (iii) Asset shown at ₹0 instead of ₹4,95,000 net book value – violates true and fair view. (iv) Tax liability artificially reduced in Year 1 (higher expense), but tax authorities may disallow excessive depreciation. The student must see that violating matching principle distorts multiple periods and legal compliance.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "If a company maintains its assets perfectly, depreciation need not be charged because the asset does not lose value." Defend your answer with reference to the causes of depreciation.
questions.a: False. Depreciation arises from (1) wear and tear from use, (2) effluxion of time (even idle assets deteriorate), (3) obsolescence (technology/market changes), and (4) expiration of legal rights. Perfect maintenance only reduces physical wear; it cannot prevent time-based deterioration, technological obsolescence, or legal expiry. AS-6 mandates depreciation for all depreciable assets regardless of maintenance. A student who agrees ignores the multi-causal nature of depreciation.

questions.q: Create a real-world scenario (Indian context) where a business purchases a fixed asset, and write a short note explaining to the owner why charging depreciation is necessary for (a) true profit, (b) tax compliance, and (c) legal requirements under the Companies Act.
questions.a: Scenario: "Ramesh buys a ₹20 lakh food delivery van for his cloud kitchen on 1-Apr-2024. Expected life: 6 years, scrap: ₹2 lakh." Note: (a) Without depreciation, Year 1 profit is understated by ₹18 lakh and Years 2–6 overstated by ₹3 lakh each – matching principle violated. (b) Income Tax Act allows depreciation deduction; skipping it increases taxable profit illegally. (c) Companies Act 2013 (Schedule II) mandates depreciation on fixed assets; non-compliance attracts penalties. A poor answer treats these as separate unrelated points instead of linking them to the core concept of cost allocation over useful life.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______ is the systematic allocation of the depreciable cost of a tangible fixed asset over its estimated useful life, representing the expired portion of the asset's cost due to usage, passage of time, or obsolescence.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you buy a ₹60,000 laptop for your freelance graphic design ______ on April 1.
What is Depreciation? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Depreciation is the systematic allocation of the depreciable cost of a tangible fixed asset over its estimated useful life, representing the expired portion of the asset's cost due to usage, passage of time, or obsolescence.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: By March ______ next year, the laptop is slower, the battery holds less charge, and newer models exist – its value has dropped.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Depreciation?
questions.a: Students believe depreciation is a valuation adjustment to bring the asset to its current market value.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to (1) define depreciation precisely using the terms "depreciable cost", "useful life", and "expired cost", (2) distinguish depreciation from depletion (natural resources) and amortisation (intangible assets) with examples, and (3) explain the four needs for depreciation: matching costs with revenue, tax.
